title: Mutable Default Argument Retains State Across Calls
symptoms: Function default list/dict accumulates data from previous invocations unexpectedly.
roast: Your ender chest keeps items from other players because you shared one default bag with the whole server.
diagnosis: Default argument expressions are evaluated once when the function definition is executed, not at each call. A mutable default like [] is shared across all calls.
debuggingSteps: Set parameter default to None: def func(items=None)
Initialize a new list inside the function body if items is None
Avoid mutable objects (lists, dicts, sets) as default parameter values
whyItWorks: Assigning None as the default and instantiating a new list inside the call ensures each invocation gets its own fresh list instance.

title: UnboundLocalError When Reassigning Variable in Outer Scope
symptoms: UnboundLocalError: local variable referenced before assignment when reading then writing a variable.
roast: Trying to craft with diamond blocks before you even mined them: Python flagged your inventory fraud.
diagnosis: If a variable is assigned anywhere inside a function body, Python marks it as local to that function for the entire scope, masking the outer variable.
debuggingSteps: Check if variable is assigned inside the function after being read
Add 'global var_name' if modifying global module state
Add 'nonlocal var_name' if modifying enclosing closure scope
badExample:
counter = 0
def increment():
    counter += 1 # UnboundLocalError: local variable 'counter' referenced before assignment
    return counter
fixedExample:
counter = 0
def increment():
    global counter
    counter += 1
    return counter
whyItWorks: Declaring 'global counter' explicitly tells the compiler that assignments target module scope rather than binding a new local variable.

title: Skipped Elements from Modifying List While Iterating
symptoms: Loop skips elements or terminates prematurely when deleting or appending elements inside a for-loop.
roast: Digging straight down while standing on the gravel block you're breaking: down into the lava you go.
diagnosis: Python list iteration tracks elements by internal index offset. Removing an element shifts subsequent elements left, causing the iterator to skip the immediate next element.
debuggingSteps: Iterate over a shallow copy of the list: for item in list(items):
Use a list comprehension to filter items into a new list
Collect items to delete and remove them in a separate pass
fixedExample:
nums = [1, 2, 2, 3]
nums = [x for x in nums if x != 2]
whyItWorks: List comprehensions create a brand new filtered list without interfering with iteration cursors.
tests: nums = [1, 2, 2, 3]; nums = [x for x in nums if x != 2]; assert nums == [1, 3]

title: Mutating Nested Collections via Shallow Copy
symptoms: Modifying a copied dictionary or list accidentally mutates the original object's nested data.
roast: Cloning your pet wolf with copy() but leaving its leash tied to your neighbor's collar.
diagnosis: Shallow copies (list.copy(), dict.copy(), copy.copy()) duplicate the top container, but nested elements remain references to the same underlying objects.
debuggingSteps: Identify nested mutable structures (lists within lists, dicts within dicts)
Import copy and use copy.deepcopy() for true isolation
Verify object identity of nested structures with id(a[0]) vs id(b[0])
badExample:
import copy
original = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = original.copy()
shallow[0].append(99) # original[0] also gets 99!
fixedExample:
import copy
original = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
deep = copy.deepcopy(original)
deep[0].append(99)
whyItWorks: copy.deepcopy recursively clones all nested objects, guaranteeing full memory decoupling.
tests: import copy; o = [[1]]; d = copy.deepcopy(o); d[0].append(2); assert len(o[0]) == 1 and len(d[0]) == 2

title: TypeError: can only concatenate str to str (not 'int')
symptoms: TypeError thrown when attempting to use '+' between a string and an integer or float.
roast: Trying to combine a book and a sword without an anvil: Python doesn't guess your recipes.
diagnosis: Python is strongly typed and does not implicitly coerce integers to strings during concatenation. Combining them requires explicit conversion or formatting.
debuggingSteps: Use modern f-strings (f'Score: {score}')
Explicitly convert with str(val)
Check data types coming from user input or APIs
whyItWorks: Formatted string literals (f-strings) automatically evaluate expressions and invoke their __format__ or __str__ representations.

title: TypeError: method takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given
symptoms: Calling an instance method on a class object throws TypeError: takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given.
roast: You told your pet to fetch, but forgot to give it ears to hear who told it.
diagnosis: Python instance method invocations implicitly pass the instance as the first argument ('self'). If the method definition omitted 'self', argument counts mismatch.
debuggingSteps: Add 'self' as the first parameter of instance methods
Or add @staticmethod decorator if the method does not access instance state
Or add @classmethod if it operates on class state
whyItWorks: Including 'self' in the parameter list binds the method to the calling object instance.
tests:
class Player: def get_health(self): return 100
assert Player().get_health() == 100

title: Generator Exhaustion When Iterating Multiple Times
symptoms: Second loop or list conversion over a generator yields empty results with no error raised.
roast: Drinking a potion of water breathing twice and wondering why the empty glass bottle gave you no bubbles.
diagnosis: Generators and iterator expressions produce values on-the-fly and maintain a one-way consumption state. Once exhausted, they yield StopIteration on all subsequent calls.
debuggingSteps: Convert the generator to a list if multiple traversals are required: items = list(gen)
Re-instantiate the generator function if lazy streaming is necessary
Inspect itertools.tee for splitting an iterator into multiple independent iterators
badExample:
gen = (x * 2 for x in range(3))
first_sum = sum(gen) # 6
second_sum = sum(gen) # 0! Generator is exhausted
fixedExample:
items = list(x * 2 for x in range(3))
first_sum = sum(items) # 6
second_sum = sum(items) # 6
whyItWorks: Materializing the generator into a list stores elements in memory, permitting repeated traversals.
tests: items = list(x * 2 for x in range(3)); assert sum(items) == 6 and sum(items) == 6

title: Using 'is' for Value Equality Instead of '=='
symptoms: Comparison fails unexpectedly for integers, strings, or floats depending on CPython interning optimizations.
roast: Checking if two swords are the same by verifying they occupy the same quantum coordinates.
diagnosis: 'is' checks identity (memory address id(a) == id(b)), while '==' checks value equality (__eq__). Using 'is' for numbers or strings produces erratic bugs when small-integer interning limits are crossed.
debuggingSteps: Use '==' for comparing values (numbers, strings, lists)
Reserve 'is' exclusively for singleton comparisons (var is None, var is True, var is False)
Run flake8 or ruff to catch SyntaxWarning / E721 lint warnings
badExample:
a = 1000
b = 1000
if a is b: # Evaluates to False in many Python environments
    pass
fixedExample:
a = 1000
b = 1000
if a == b: # Evaluates to True reliably
    pass
whyItWorks: '==' invokes the __eq__ method, comparing numeric values rather than underlying memory pointers.

title: Late Binding Closures in Loops Producing Uniform Values
symptoms: All lambdas created inside a loop evaluate with the final loop iteration variable value.
roast: Printing 5 name tags inside a loop, but all of them say 'Creeper #5' because you only filled the ink at the end.
diagnosis: Python closures bind variables by reference, not by value. The closure looks up 'i' at call time, when the loop has already completed and 'i' holds its final value.
debuggingSteps: Bind the loop variable eagerly using default arguments: lambda x, i=i: x + i
Use functools.partial to freeze arguments
Define an enclosing helper function to create a distinct scope
badExample:
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
results = [f() for f in funcs] # Produces [2, 2, 2] instead of [0, 1, 2]!
fixedExample:
funcs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
results = [f() for f in funcs] # Produces [0, 1, 2]
whyItWorks: Default arguments are evaluated when the lambda is created, snapshotting the current value of i into the function closure's default tuple.
tests: funcs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]; assert [f() for f in funcs] == [0, 1, 2]

title: Catching Bare 'except:' Swallowing KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
symptoms: Script cannot be stopped with Ctrl+C, or exit commands are trapped and ignored.
roast: Building an indestructible bedrock bunker that traps yourself inside forever: you can't even quit the world.
diagnosis: A bare 'except:' catches BaseException, which includes KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit. This prevents graceful cancellation or termination.
debuggingSteps: Catch 'except Exception:' instead of bare 'except:' to allow system signals to propagate
Catch specific error classes (ValueError, KeyError, IOError) whenever possible
Rethrow unexpected exceptions with 'raise'
whyItWorks: Inheriting from Exception allows system exit events like KeyboardInterrupt (which inherit directly from BaseException) to pass through unimpeded.
tests:
try: raise ValueError('err')
except Exception as e: assert isinstance(e, ValueError)
